items.title: The Phillips curve broke down spectacularly in the 1970s
items.claim: Bill Phillips's 1958 paper documented an inverse relationship between UK unemployment and wage inflation. What happened in the 1970s?

options.text: The relationship held perfectly, vindicating Keynesian demand management
The US and UK experienced 'stagflation' — high inflation AND high unemployment simultaneously, which the simple Phillips curve said was impossible
The relationship inverted entirely; lower unemployment led to deflation
Statistical data became unreliable, so no test was possible

items.reveal:
The 1970s combined oil shocks (1973, 1979), wage-price spirals and weak productivity growth. US inflation reached 13.5% in 1980; unemployment was 7.5%. Both up, together.

Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps had argued in the late 1960s that the long-run Phillips curve was vertical at the 'natural rate' of unemployment — once expectations adjusted, only the natural rate was stable. The 1970s vindicated them and supplied the intellectual ammunition for monetarism, Volcker and Thatcher.

Modern expectations-augmented Phillips curves are still used but are far less crisp than the original.
items.why: The Phillips curve example is the cleanest case of a model that worked, then didn't. It's also why mid-20th-century Keynesianism gave way to monetarism, with consequences that still shape macro policy.

items.title: Switching costs create lock-in even without monopoly
items.claim: Mobile phone contracts, banking services and software subscriptions all create switching costs. How does this affect competition?

options.text: High switching costs reduce price elasticity, allow price discrimination, and create incumbency advantages; competition can shift from price-on-price to acquisition incentives that don't always benefit existing customers
Switching costs only exist in monopoly

items.reveal:
Klemperer's research (1987 onwards) formalised switching cost economics. UK's Open Banking initiative (2018), CASS (Current Account Switch Service 2013) and Ofcom's text-to-switch (2019) all aim to reduce switching frictions specifically.

The CMA's 2016 retail banking market investigation found switching costs and informational frictions sustained higher prices and weak competition.
items.why: Competition exists on a spectrum shaped by frictions. Policy can target the frictions directly (lower switching costs) rather than only firm conduct.

items.title: The UK's 2010-2015 austerity programme
items.claim: The UK government under Osborne (2010-2016) pursued fiscal consolidation. What was the actual deficit reduction trajectory?

options.text: Budget deficit fell from ~10% of GDP (2009-10) to ~4% by 2015-16, but the target of eliminating it by 2015 was missed; growth was slower than OBR projections; public investment was cut sharply

items.reveal:
ONS data: UK fiscal deficit was 10.1% of GDP in 2009-10, 4.1% by 2015-16. The original 2010 emergency budget aimed to balance the structural deficit by 2015; the target was slipped repeatedly.

IFS and OBR analyses found growth fell short of pre-austerity forecasts. Economic historians (Blyth 'Austerity', 2013) and IMF research raised doubts about the timing of consolidation; defenders (Niemietz, others) argued the policy preserved fiscal credibility.

The austerity debate continues; the empirical record is contested but the speed of recovery was slower than baseline.
items.why: Major macroeconomic policy choices have decade-long effects that are hard to evaluate cleanly because counterfactuals are unobservable.
